headline: Senators Ricketts and Klobuchar split on 11 December hemp THC ban
dek: With four weeks left before most hemp THC products lose federal legality, a Nebraska Republican wants no more delay and a Minnesota Democrat wants a fix.
key_points: Sen. Pete Ricketts (R-NE) wrote on 12 November that the September delay of the hemp THC ban was a mistake and that the Senate should close the loophole for good.
Sen. Amy Klobuchar (D-MN) said a day later she is working on a bipartisan fix, after leading the push that moved the deadline from 12 November to 11 December.
Minnesota's regulated hemp THC market sold about $180 million last year, with most products at 5mg per serving, far above the federal 0.4mg-per-container cap.
No floor vote on a further delay or a regulatory framework had been scheduled as of 13 November.
body: Two senators set out opposite answers this week to the question the hemp industry has four weeks to settle: should Congress let its ban on most intoxicating hemp products take effect on 11 December, or replace it with rules? Sen. Pete Ricketts, a Nebraska Republican, argued in a Fox News op-ed on 12 November that the delay Congress approved in September was a mistake and that the Senate must close what he calls the THC loophole once and for all.

A day later Sen. Amy Klobuchar, a Minnesota Democrat who led that delay, said she is fighting for a bipartisan fix, according to Marijuana Moment's 13 November newsletter. The split is not neatly partisan: the delay survived a Senate vote of 61 to 32 in August, which means a large bloc of Republicans backed it. What happens next decides whether thousands of shops in states that regulate hemp THC, Minnesota among them, can keep selling drinks and edibles after mid-December.

The law at issue is the hemp redefinition Congress attached to the November 2025 deal that reopened the government. It removes products with more than 0.4 milligrams of total THC per container from the federal definition of hemp, which CBS Minnesota said effectively bans the drinks and edibles now on shelves. The change was due on 12 November 2026.

In September Congress split it in two. Klobuchar's office said the stopgap spending bill moved the deadline for most products to 11 December and banned synthetic hemp derivatives, based on the Hemp Planting Predictability Act she wrote with Sen. Rand Paul, a Kentucky Republican. As we reported on 12 November, that first, narrower phase took effect on schedule: cannabinoids the plant cannot make naturally are now off the federal hemp list. The broader 0.4mg cap is what arrives on 11 December.

Ricketts signed Nebraska's hemp farming law as governor to line the state up with the 2018 Farm Bill, and he wrote that the results were drastically different from what he expected. In his telling, the Farm Bill let manufacturers sell delta-8 and delta-10 THC in packaging that mimics candy, sodas and chips, at gas stations and smoke shops with no age limit.

He cited a Journal of the American Medical Association finding that more than one in ten high school seniors have used hemp-derived THC, a case in Omaha in which two small children ate gummies and recovered, and a rise of more than 1,000 percent in reported accidental THC poisonings among children under five. Those are his figures as stated in the op-ed. He praised Nebraska Attorney General Mike Hilgers for cracking down on the products, and said the industry had already been given a full year to comply.
> The 11 December fight is no longer about whether hemp THC gets rules; it is about whether Congress writes them before the cap lands or after.

Klobuchar's argument rests on states that chose to regulate rather than ban. Minnesota legalised hemp-derived THC edibles in 2022 with a 5mg-per-serving limit, and CBS Minnesota reported that retail sales of the products hit $180 million last year. A typical 5mg serving is about 12 times the 0.4mg the federal law will allow in a whole container, so almost nothing on Minnesota shelves would survive the cap.

In a statement to WCCO, Klobuchar said Congress must pass bipartisan legislation to give producers, retailers and customers certainty. She said she has introduced several bills with Paul and is working with Sen. Tim Sheehy, a Montana Republican, on another. An industry advocate quoted by the station said he is lobbying Congress and still hopes for a deal before the deadline.

The lobbying is getting more visible. Marijuana Moment reported on 13 November that a consulting firm run by the daughter of former White House chief of staff Susie Wiles was paid $15,000 by the political fund of Hemp Industry and Farmers of America. The report did not say what the work involved, and there is no suggestion in it of wrongdoing.

The politics are also shifting. Democrats will hold at least 55 Senate seats next year after the midterms, NBC News projected, but the new Congress is not sworn in until January, after the deadline. As we reported on 11 November, the Senate's draft FY2027 agriculture spending bill funds hemp programmes but leaves the 11 December cap in place, so the vehicle for any change in the next four weeks is not yet obvious.

For licensed cannabis companies, the cap is a potential gain: as we reported on 13 November, Missouri and Illinois now route over-limit products into dispensaries. For hemp brands, the planning question is whether to keep inventory moving into December or wind down now. Products that comply with the 0.4mg cap remain federally legal, and state law still applies on top of the federal rule.

Ricketts wrote with an eye on the Senate's return to Washington this month. Watch for a stand-alone hemp regulation bill or a delay attached to year-end spending legislation, and for whether Sheehy's proposal with Klobuchar is filed. In Illinois, a federal judge hears the hemp industry's challenge to the state's cap on 19 November. Unless Congress acts, the federal 0.4mg limit takes effect on 11 December.
